doc.title: Jon Jang interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, September 17, 2003 [interview 1 of 2]

chapter: Career, market and the state of jazz
title: Versatility, a possible trio, and the jazz market's demand for familiarity
summary: Billy Taylor's advice to tell his stories as pianist, the impracticality of touring the sextet, and presenters wanting standard repertory.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Managers, bookers and the business of getting work

blocks.x: Well your concern is something that I have seriously considered. And that’s why I think I do have to have multiple ways to, like the other question to survive. And I don’t think I could just survive just doing that kind of music. But that doesn’t mean that I’m going to — I mean there’s other ways to see Jon Jang because I’m very versatile. And one of the weaknesses I’ve had over the years is because I’ve had to create all these ambitious projects with such great artists that my voice as a pianist has been suppressed. Because I can perform in a lot of kind of situations because I’ve had diverse experiences. So Billy Taylor, I’ve collaborated with him at the Asia Society of New York in 1995 with taiko performer Kenny Endo from Hawaii, and we did part of a series called “Crossovers.” And it was collaborations with Asian traditional music and jazz. And Dr. Taylor told me that, “You know Jon you have some important stories to tell.” And I thought about it and I said yeah but my present projects, which are really not tourable. I mean the Jon Jang sextet, that with Billy Hart, David Murray and James Newton, six great artists, and then I’m not doing jazz repertory music, and they’re all busy. It’s not practical. So now I’m kind of looking at well yeah Billy Taylor has, I’m not saying that I will do what Billy Taylor does, but maybe I need to have like a trio that features my voice as a pianist and then I could tell stories like the way Dr. Taylor does. Because you see that there is no Chinese traditional music. Because actually there’s been problems working with Chinese traditional musicians because if they’re unable to perform with you because they have other commitments then where do you go to get Chinese traditional musicians? And then if you do find them, they’re not used to performing in that context. So I think I’ve done some important work that hasn’t been done but in terms of it having an impact — well in terms of like audiences it’s limited. I mean you can look back and say yeah this is important in terms of posterity, but it’s like there’s certain survival — what about me trying to sustain that. And also I think some of these projects, there isn’t an organic — I mean the residencies have been important in terms of incubating so that great — but then you don’t get to that level where if you’re performing every night or on a consistent level at least once every two weeks with those ensembles or new works, then you can’t take that music to another level.
Would you feel comfortable for instance trying to book a trio gig at, is it Yoshi’s in Oakland? Is that the jazz club there?

Yeah, I mean I’ve performed there as a sextet. And actually I did do a trio, but I don’t think I had my concept of the kind of music I was going to do. It hadn’t developed. It hadn’t emerged. But so I have to think about that. And if I wanted to be in the jazz market I probably would have to do standard repertory. I don’t know if I would do that. I mean I did perform an Ellington program with “Clothed Woman” and some works that are not part of what I call quote unquote Ellington standards, but some of the lesser known works that are incredible works themselves that I like, I enjoy it. But I’m not sure if I would want to tour with it or commit to that. So if you want to be part of the jazz market you have to do that kind of — like presenters, especially in a period where they’re uncomfortable, they’re worried about the box office and the revenues and particularly in this economy, they want something that’s familiar, and they know people are going to come. If you keep changing your face, like well what is Jon Jang doing now, it’s a chameleon, then they feel very uncomfortable. “Oh I thought I saw you do that last year and now you’re doing this.”
How am I going to book that and bill that.

And then sometimes in the jazz market they want to hear you perform. It’s not — they don’t want to hear a new work. They want to hear somebody that can play, for whatever reason. They want to hear the experience of this performer or that song, like it was on the recording.

They want to hear “Take the A String.” That’s part of an inside joke that no-one knows what we’re talking about but it was a good joke on your part actually. You know you said something interesting. A student apparently had asked you about the state or the future of jazz. And you were saying you think there’s a disconnect between the current young generation and what has come before. Did I say that right?
